name: Annual change in the foreign-born population of the United States
descriptionProcessing: We calculated the change between each pair of consecutive censuses or surveys and divided it by the number of years between them. Every year of an interval shows this average annual change.
datasetName: Historical Census Statistics on the Foreign-Born Population of the United States: 1850 to 2000
descriptionKey:
This indicator shows how much the foreign-born population grew or shrank each year. The change combines people arriving, people leaving, and deaths among the foreign-born, so it is not a count of new immigrants.

Before 2005, the data comes from censuses taken every ten years (and a first survey estimate in 2005), so the change cannot be calculated for single years. Over those periods, we divide the measured change evenly across the years: for example, each year of the 1850s shows one tenth of the change between the 1850 and 1860 censuses. There is no estimate for 2020, so the values for 2020 and 2021 each show half of the change between 2019 and 2021.

The change between 2000 and 2005 compares a census count with a survey estimate, so part of it may reflect the switch in method rather than a real change in the population. From 2006 onward, the change compares two survey estimates; small year-to-year changes can be within the survey's margin of error.

The foreign-born population covers everyone living in the United States who was not a US citizen at birth, whatever their current legal status. People born in the United States, in its territories such as Puerto Rico, or abroad to American parents count as native-born.

The data comes from two sources with the same definition of foreign-born:
- **1850–2000:** the decennial census. Figures up to 1940 come from a full count of the population; figures from 1950 to 2000 are based on large census samples (between 1 in 4 and 1 in 6 people).
- **2005 onward:** the American Community Survey, an annual survey of about 3.5 million households. Survey estimates are less exact than a census count.

Two things changed over the course of the series:
- The population included: Alaska and Hawaii are included from 1960 onward. The 1890 figures exclude about 325,000 people living in the Indian Territory and on Indian reservations, who were not asked about their place of birth.
- The list of US territories: people born in a territory count as native-born, so when a territory's status changed, so did their classification. For example, people born in the Philippines counted as native-born until it became independent in 1946, and as foreign-born after.

People living in the country without authorization are included in the definition, but censuses and surveys are known to miss part of this group. Other sources that try to adjust for this can find a slightly higher foreign-born population.

origins.title: Historical Census Statistics on the Foreign-Born Population of the United States: 1850 to 2000
origins.descriptionSnapshot: Table 1 of the report, which gives the total population and the foreign-born population of the United States at each census from 1850 to 2000. The foreign-born population covers everyone living in the United States who was not a US citizen at birth, whatever their legal status.
origins.description: A report by the US Census Bureau that brings together statistics on the foreign-born population of the United States from every census between 1850 and 2000. Its tables cover nativity, citizenship, place of birth, language, age and sex, race and Hispanic origin, length of residence, and place of residence.
origins.citationFull: Gibson, Campbell and Kay Jung. 2006. Historical Census Statistics on the Foreign-Born Population of the United States: 1850 to 2000. Population Division Working Paper No. 81. Washington, DC: U.S. Census Bureau.

origins.titleSnapshot: American Community Survey - Nativity of the population
origins.title: American Community Survey
origins.descriptionSnapshot: This file contains the total population and the foreign-born population of the United States for each year from 2005, from the ACS 1-year estimates (table B05002, "Place of Birth by Nativity and Citizenship Status"), retrieved through the Census Bureau data API. The foreign-born population covers everyone living in the United States who was born in another country, whatever their legal status. There is no value for 2020: the Census Bureau did not release standard 1-year estimates for that year because of data-collection problems during the COVID-19 pandemic.
origins.description: The American Community Survey (ACS) is an annual survey run by the US Census Bureau. It samples about 3.5 million housing unit addresses each year and measures the demographic, social, economic, and housing characteristics of the US population. Since 2005, it has replaced the long-form questionnaire of the decennial census.
origins.citationFull: U.S. Census Bureau, American Community Survey 1-Year Estimates, Table B05002 (Place of Birth by Nativity and Citizenship Status).
